title: Psalm 36: The Fountain of Life
summary: The psalm begins by describing the wicked man, who has no fear of God, flatters himself, and plots evil even in bed. It then turns abruptly to the LORD, whose loving devotion reaches the heavens and whose house offers refuge, feasting, and the fountain of life. It closes with a prayer that God keep extending his love to the upright and a vision of the evildoers fallen.
story: After the courtroom struggle of Psalm 35, Psalm 36 steps back to contrast two ways of living: the self-deceived path of the wicked and the life that drinks from God's abundance. It holds together the dark realism of the Psalms about human evil and their bright confidence in God's goodness. Paul quotes its first verse as the final charge in his catalog of human sin in Romans 3, and the rest of the psalm supplies some of the Bible's most memorable images of God's generosity: the shadow of his wings, the river of delights, the fountain of life, light in his light.
historical:
The heading calls David the servant of the LORD, a title that appears in a psalm heading only here and in Psalm 18. The title is given elsewhere to Moses, Joshua, and David (for example 2 Samuel 7 and many prophetic passages), and it marks someone God has chosen for a task. The psalm gives no clue to a specific event. Scholars differ on whether David wrote it or whether the heading places it within a Davidic collection used in the temple; many classify it as a mixture of wisdom reflection and lament.

The mention of God's house in verse 8 suggests the temple or, before it was built, the tabernacle, as the place where God's people feasted in his presence. Some scholars think the psalm was used in temple worship, where the images of refuge, feast, and river would have had concrete counterparts in the sanctuary's courts, sacrificial meals, and water basins.
cultural:
Verse 1 uses a word normally reserved for prophetic speech, an oracle, which the prophets used for a declaration of the LORD. Here it is transgression that speaks, whispering to the wicked man deep within. The Hebrew of verse 1 is difficult, and translations differ over whether the oracle is in the psalmist's heart or the wicked man's; the BSB takes it as the psalmist's inner insight about the wicked.

The shadow of Your wings (verse 7) is an image found several times in the Psalms and in Ruth 2:12. Some interpreters see a mother bird sheltering her young; others think of the outstretched wings of the cherubim over the ark in the Most Holy Place, which would fit the reference to God's house in the next verse. Feasting on the abundance of the house recalls the sacrificial meals Israelites ate in the sanctuary, where part of the offering was shared with the worshiper. In a dry land where water meant life, a flowing river and a fountain were images of lavish provision. The word for delights in verse 8 shares its root with the name Eden.
literary: The psalm has three parts. Verses 1 to 4 portray the wicked man from the inside out: his eyes, his mouth, his bed, and his path. Verses 5 to 9 turn to God with a hymn that moves up to the heavens and clouds, out to the mountains and the deep sea, and then into the house, the river, the fountain, and the light. Verses 10 to 12 are a short prayer and a closing vision. The contrast is sharp: the wicked man plots on his bed, while God's guests feast in his house; the wicked man ceases to be wise, while God's people see light in his light. The words There the evildoers lie fallen in verse 12 end the psalm with a single picture, as though the psalmist can already see the outcome.

outline.t: The inner life of the wicked: no fear of God
The LORD's love, faithfulness, righteousness, and judgments
Refuge, feast, river, fountain, and light
Prayer for continued love and protection from the proud

doctrines.note: Verses 1 to 4 describe sin as self-deception: the wicked man flatters himself too much to see his own wrongdoing. Sin begins with the absence of the fear of God and ends with a settled path that no longer rejects evil.

The psalm piles up God's attributes with images of vast scale: loving devotion reaching the heavens, faithfulness to the clouds, righteousness like mountains, judgments like the deep sea. God's character is greater than the whole visible world.
Verse 9 locates life itself in God: with You is the fountain of life. Salvation is pictured as coming to his house, taking refuge under his wings, and receiving life and light from him.

words.note: Ne'um, oracle or declaration. Almost everywhere in the Old Testament it introduces the words of the LORD through a prophet (declares the LORD). Its use in verse 1 for the whisper of transgression is startling and probably ironic: sin speaks to the wicked with the authority he should have given God's word.

Maqor, fountain or spring. In Jeremiah 2:13 the LORD calls himself the fountain of living water, abandoned by his people for cracked cisterns. In verse 9 the fountain of life is with God. The image is of a source that never runs dry, not stored water but a flowing spring.

Eden, delight or luxury. The river of delights in verse 8 uses the same letters as the garden of Eden, and many interpreters hear an echo of the river that watered Eden (Genesis 2:10). God's house is pictured as a place where the abundance of the first garden is found again.

christ: Paul quotes verse 1, that there is no fear of God before his eyes, as the last line of his long indictment in Romans 3:10-18, which shows that all people, Jew and Gentile, are under sin. The psalm's second half points in the other direction, toward the source of life and light in God. The New Testament identifies that source with Christ: in John's Gospel, in him was life, and that life was the light of men (John 1:4), and Jesus offers living water (John 4:10-14; 7:37-38). These are thematic connections rather than predictions, but they show how the psalm's images of God's generosity find a face in Jesus, who also used the picture of a hen gathering her chicks under her wings (Matthew 23:37).
questions: Verse 2 says the wicked man is too full of conceit to detect his own sin. How can a person guard against that kind of self-deception?
Which image of God's goodness in verses 7 to 9 speaks most to you right now, and why?
In Your light we see light. How has knowing God changed the way you see other things?
